procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated June 20, 1969 of the Delhi High Court at New Delhi in Criminal Revision No. 385 of 1968, which restored the order of sentence passed by the Trial Magistrate.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Municipal Corporation filed a revision petition in the High Court urging that the Additional Sessions Judge should not have reduced the sentence imposed by the Trial Magistrate. The High Court accepted that contention, setting aside the Additional Sessions Judge's order and restoring the Trial Magistrate's sentence. The High Court granted a certificate under Art. 134 (c) of the Constitution.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant filed an appeal in the Supreme Court on the strength of the certificate granted by the High Court. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal because the appellant's counsel did not challenge the conviction or sentence, only raising a point about a previous similar offense.

issue.issue_text: Whether Section 4 of the Probation of Offenders Act should be applied to release the appellant from the mandatory minimum sentence of imprisonment prescribed under Section 16 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act.

facts: The appellant, an employee of a sweetmeat shop, was convicted under the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act.
He was found guilty of selling 'patisa' (a sweet) that was adulterated with an unpermitted coal tar dye.
He was sentenced to the mandatory minimum of six months simple imprisonment and a fine of one thousand rupees as prescribed by Section 16 of the Act.
law: Section 16 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act imposes a mandatory minimum sentence for selling adulterated food.
Section 4 of the Probation of Offenders Act gives courts the discretion to release an offender on probation instead of imposing a prison sentence.

A prior Supreme Court decision (*Isherdas v. Punjab*) established that the Probation of Offenders Act can apply to food adulteration cases, but it should not be used lightly because food adulteration is a menace to public health and an anti-social evil.
application: The Court characterized the appellant's act of selling food with an unpermitted dye as a "distinctly anti-social" activity.

It reasoned that the dye was used to attract customers without any regard for the potential injury it could cause to consumers, particularly children and non-affluent individuals who often purchase such items.
The Court emphasized that the primary objective of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act is to eradicate such harmful, anti-social practices and ensure the purity of food.
Applying the Probation of Offenders Act in this instance would contradict and undermine the specific legislative intent of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that it would be neither expedient nor in line with the object of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act to apply Section 4 of the Probation of Offenders Act. Given the anti-social nature of the crime and its danger to public health, the mandatory minimum sentence was upheld, and the request to release the appellant on probation was rejected.

arguments.issue_text: Whether Section 4 of the Probation of Offenders Act should be applied to release the appellant from the mandatory minimum sentence of imprisonment prescribed under Section 16 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act.
appellant_arguments: The appellant should be given the benefit of Section 4 of the Probation of Offenders Act, 1958, which would allow the court to dispense with the sentence of imprisonment and issue an admonition instead.
respondent_arguments: In view of the mandatory provisions of Section 16 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, which provides for a compulsory minimum sentence, the court ought not to interfere with or reduce the sentence of imprisonment imposed by the Trial Magistrate.

cases.principle: The operation of the Probation of Offenders Act is not excluded in cases under the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: An article of food is deemed adulterated under Section 2(i)(j) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act if it contains a non-permissible coloring matter, irrespective of whether the article is proven to be injurious to health. The sale of such an article mandates the minimum sentence prescribed by Section 16 of the Act, as the proviso allowing for sentencing discretion is not applicable to this category of adulteration.
obiter: Courts should not lightly resort to the provisions of the Probation of Offenders Act in cases involving the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The sale of an article of food prepared with an unpermitted coal tar dye is a distinctly anti-social activity, deleterious to the health of consumers, particularly children and the non-affluent. The principal aim of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act is the eradication of this evil. Therefore, it would be neither expedient nor in consonance with the object of the Act to apply Section 4 of the Probation of Offenders Act to release the appellant from the mandatory sentence of imprisonment.
legal_tests_applied: Whether, in the circumstances of the case and the nature of the evil the statute was enacted to prevent, it is expedient and in consonance with the object of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act to apply Section 4 of the Probation of Offenders Act.

While the Probation of Offenders Act is not excluded in cases under the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, courts should not lightly resort to its provisions, as adulteration of food is a menace to public health.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's activity of selling food with an unpermitted coal tar dye was deemed a "distinctly anti-social" act.
Applying the Probation of Offenders Act would not be "in consonance with the object with which the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act was passed," which is the eradication of such anti-social evils.

The court presumed the unpermitted coal tar dye was injurious to health, stating: "Though there was no express evidence on the record that the use of the part'.cular coal tar dye...was injurious to health, it must be presumed to be so from the fact that it is not one of the permitted coal tar dyes enumerated in r. 28."
The court found the evil to be "more pernicious" because the victims were often "child:en and by persons from the unaftluent sections of the wciety."
why_respondent_won: The court affirmed that the policy of Section 16 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act is to impose a mandatory minimum sentence for the sale of food adulterated under Section 2(i)(j).
The court characterized the offense as a serious "menace to public health" and an "anti-social evil," justifying the imposition of the prescribed sentence.
The court concluded that the eradication of the sale of such deleterious food items is the "principal aim of the Act and in particular of s. 16 thereof," which militated against leniency.
policy_considerations: Adulteration of food is a menace to public health, and the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act was enacted with the object of eradicating that anti-social evil and ensuring the purity of food sold to the public.
The court should not lightly resort to the provisions of the Probation of Offenders Act in food adulteration cases, as it would undermine the legislative intent to combat this public health threat.
The court must consider the vulnerability of the consumers, noting that such adulterated sweets are often purchased by children and non-affluent sections of society.
The motive for the adulteration, which was to "attract customers, without any regard to the injury it would cause to these who consumed them," reinforces the anti-social nature of the crime.
